statement: The Procurement Act 2023 provides two competitive tendering procedures. The open procedure is a single-stage process in which any interested party may submit a tender; the contracting authority evaluates all tenders received and awards accordingly. It is available for most public contracts and is the simpler of the two routes.

The competitive flexible procedure replaces the former restricted procedure, competitive procedure with negotiation, and competitive dialogue. It permits any multi-stage design the authority considers appropriate, including pre-qualification, negotiation, dialogue, or demonstration stages. It is mandatory where the authority wishes to limit supplier numbers before issuing a tender invitation, when procuring under a dynamic market, or when reserving a contract to supported employment providers or public service mutuals.

A standard (closed) framework may not exceed 4 years for general public contracts. The maximum is 8 years for defence/security frameworks and utilities frameworks. A longer term is permitted only where the nature of the goods, services, or works to be supplied under call-off contracts specifically requires it, and that justification must be documented.

topic: Frameworks — open frameworks (max 8 years; must reopen to new suppliers)
statement: An open framework is a scheme of successive frameworks awarded on substantially the same terms (s.49). It has an overall maximum duration of 8 years from the first award. The authority must reopen the framework to competition at least once in the first 3 years and at least once every 5 years thereafter, allowing new suppliers to compete in each cycle. If only one supplier is awarded a framework within the scheme, both that framework and the open framework scheme must terminate within 4 years of that award.

topic: Framework call-offs — direct award within framework vs statutory direct award
statement: A framework call-off awarded without competition (under an objective mechanism such as a taxi-rank or highest-ranked rotation in the framework terms — s.45(3-4)) is NOT a statutory direct award under sections 41 or 43. The guidance states explicitly: 'Direct award under sections 41 or 43 cannot be used to award a call-off contract under a framework and is unnecessary.' Call-offs follow the framework regime's own selection process and are procedurally distinct from the direct award provisions that require a Schedule 5 justification.

The Act abolishes Dynamic Purchasing Systems (DPS) and Qualification Systems, replacing both with a single commercial tool called a 'dynamic market'. Unlike DPS, a dynamic market must remain open to new suppliers at all times, may be used for any procurement (not just commonly-used purchases), and contracts under it must be awarded using the competitive flexible procedure. The conditions for membership cannot be modified during the market's life.

topic: Dynamic markets — existing DPS transitional end date (23 February 2029)
statement: DPS established under the previous Public Contracts Regulations 2015 are deemed to continue under saving provisions but must terminate by 23 February 2029 at the latest, or on their originally scheduled end date if earlier. DPS may only be extended within the first 12 months after the Act came into force (24 February 2025) and cannot be extended beyond the February 2029 long-stop date.

topic: Direct award — Schedule 5 grounds and transparency notice requirement (s.41/s.44)
statement: A contracting authority may award a public contract directly (without competitive tendering) only where a Schedule 5 direct-award justification applies (s.41). The main grounds are: (i) prototype or early development (novel goods/services designed at the authority's request); (ii) single-supplier — exclusive IP/rights or technical reasons prevent competition; (iii) additional/repeat supplies from existing supplier where switching causes disproportionate technical difficulties, or repeat within 5 years of a competitively-tendered contract; (iv) commodities purchased on commodity markets; (v) advantageous insolvency terms; (vi) extreme and unavoidable urgency not attributable to the authority; (vii) user-choice light-touch services where the individual selects the supplier; (viii) specific defence/security grounds. Before awarding, the authority must publish a transparency notice on the central digital platform (s.44), stating the intended supplier (if known), the Schedule 5 ground relied on, the justification, and any known modification risks. Exception: user-choice contracts (Schedule 5, para. 15) are exempt from the transparency notice.

topic: Mandatory 8-working-day standstill after contract award notice (s.51)
statement: After a competitive procurement, the authority must publish a contract award notice on the central digital platform and then observe a mandatory standstill period of at least 8 working days before signing the contract (s.51). Working day 1 is the day the notice is published; the contract may not be entered into before working day 9. Exceptions where standstill does not apply: (a) extreme urgency direct awards, (b) protect-life direct awards (s.42), (c) contracts awarded by private utilities, (d) call-off contracts under frameworks, (e) dynamic market contracts, (f) light touch contracts. Authorities may impose a voluntary standstill (also minimum 8 working days) for exempt categories. A legal challenge notified during the standstill triggers automatic suspension preventing signing until the challenge is resolved.

topic: KPI duty — publish at least 3 KPIs for contracts above £5 million (s.52)
statement: For any public contract with an estimated value exceeding £5 million, the contracting authority must set at least 3 key performance indicators before entering into the contract and must publish them (s.52). KPIs must be assessed at least annually during the contract's life and on termination; results must be published in a contract performance notice using standardised ratings. The duty does not apply to frameworks themselves (though call-off contracts over £5m are caught), utilities contracts awarded by private utilities, concession contracts, or light touch contracts. Authorities may disapply the requirement only if they can demonstrate that supplier performance under the specific contract could not appropriately be assessed by reference to KPIs.

Contracting authorities must exclude suppliers meeting mandatory grounds in Schedule 6: criminal convictions for corporate manslaughter, terrorism, fraud, bribery, slavery, cartel offences, tax evasion, and organised crime; non-conviction grounds including HMRC tax misconduct, CMA cartel decisions, and national security determinations. Authorities may exclude suppliers on Schedule 7 discretionary grounds: labour market misconduct, environmental offences, insolvency, professional misconduct, poor past performance, or competition concerns. A supplier can avoid exclusion by self-cleaning (s.58): demonstrating through concrete evidence — compensation paid, procedural reforms, staff changes, SMART future commitments — that the circumstances are not continuing and not likely to recur. The standard lookback period is 5 years.

topic: Debarment register — s.62 central list; duty to check before every covered procurement
statement: Section 62 empowers a Minister to maintain a central debarment list of suppliers that meet exclusion grounds and whose circumstances are continuing or likely to recur. The list must be published and is available to all contracting authorities. Contracting authorities have a statutory duty to check the debarment list before allowing any supplier to participate in a covered procurement. Suppliers on the list under mandatory grounds must be excluded (limited public-interest override applies). Before listing, the Minister must give the supplier 8 working days' written notice. Contracting authorities that exclude a supplier must notify the relevant Minister within 30 days.

topic: Payment-method-blind scope — GPC / purchase cards do not disapply PA2023
statement: The Procurement Act 2023 applies to any public contract for the supply of goods, services, or works for pecuniary interest that exceeds the relevant threshold and is not Schedule 2-exempt (s.3). The trigger is contract value and type, not the payment mechanism used. Neither the Act nor its official guidance provides any exemption based on payment method. Paying via a Government Procurement Card (GPC), purchase card, or any other payment instrument does not reduce or remove the authority's obligations under the Act. The Schedule 2 exemptions are exhaustive and relate entirely to contract type and counterparty relationships; payment method appears nowhere in them.

topic: Thresholds — when PA2023 applies (Schedule 1, as amended)
statement: The Act applies to covered procurement above the following estimated-value thresholds (Schedule 1, current as of 2025): central government authorities — £135,018 for goods/services; sub-central authorities — £207,720; works contracts — £5,193,000; light touch services — £663,540; utilities goods/services — £415,440; utilities and defence/security works — £5,193,000. Contracts below threshold are subject to lighter-touch rules under Part 6 but are not fully covered procurement. Contract value must be estimated over the whole term, including all options and renewals, to determine whether the threshold is met.

topic: Transition — procurements commenced before 24 February 2025 remain under PCR 2015
statement: Procurements commenced (i.e. a tender notice published) before 24 February 2025 must continue to be conducted and managed under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (or other predecessor legislation) through to contract conclusion, including any modifications or termination. Only procurements commenced on or after 24 February 2025 are governed by the Procurement Act 2023. A buyer running a live PCR 2015 process should not switch to PA2023 rules mid-process.
